blocks.cap: The kitchen of the Uedera flat before four in the morning

blocks.p: The plate was still upside down on the counter.

Rei stood in the dark kitchen and looked at it. A white plate turned over a second plate, the way he had left it at nine o'clock. Under it, rice and the ginger pork Gin liked, gone cold and grey. Nobody had lifted it. Nobody had eaten.
He was holding the kettle. He did not remember picking it up. The clock on the stove said 3:47.

The flat had the silence of two rooms built for two people and holding only one. Outside, Tokyo had reached the hour when even the trucks go quiet. Somewhere below, a vending machine hummed to itself on the corner of the street.

Gin kept strange hours. Everyone who knew Uedera Gin knew that. He was twenty-eight, nine years older than Rei, a field officer for the Civil Veil Division, and his work did not stop at five. But he called. He always called. Ten minutes late meant a message. An hour late meant a phone call and a voice saying, “Eat without me, I'm fine, go to bed.” In nineteen years he had never once let a night close over him without a word.

Rei checked his phone. No message. He checked it again, because lately he checked everything twice. The lock. The stove. The date. For a few weeks now the city had felt to him like a held breath, and he had told nobody, because there was nothing to tell. Just a feeling. Just a habit he did not like.

In the black glass of the window his own face looked back at him. Tired eyes. A jaw more Gin's than his own. Rei, he thought, to make the reflection agree to the name. It agreed. He did not know why that felt like a relief.
He switched on the living-room lamp. He never did that at night. Lately the dark had started to feel as if it was paying attention, and he wanted it to stop.
Gin's door was shut. Rei knocked once, softly, feeling stupid, and opened it.

blocks.cap: Gin's room, the bed made and the desk lamp burning

blocks.p: The bed was made with square corners. The chair was pushed all the way under the desk. And the desk lamp was on. A small yellow circle lay on the bare wood, as though Gin had been working under it a minute ago and stepped out to take a call. Nothing lay in the circle. No pen, no paper, no cup.

On the shelf above the desk stood the spine of the notebook Gin wrote in at night and always closed when Rei came near. Propped against the base of the lamp was a photograph of the two of them years ago, squinting into the sun on some beach Rei could barely remember. Gin kept it where he could see it from the bed.

The room did not feel empty. It felt left. Rei could not tell whether that was true or whether he was doing what Gin had always warned him about, finding shapes in the quiet because the quiet frightened him.
Back in the kitchen he filled the kettle and did not light the gas. Two cups sat upside down on the rack. Gin always set out two, though he was never home for the second.
Then Rei looked at the hook by the front door, and his stomach went cold.
Gin's keys were not on it.

They had hung there every day since Rei was small enough to be lifted up to reach them. Gin put them on the hook first thing every morning, before coffee, before anything, the way some people touch a doorframe for luck. The brass hook was worn bright where his thumb went. Rei had a private joke about it. Some mornings he slid the keys a few centimetres along the hook to see whether Gin would notice. Gin never said a word. Rei had always taken that to mean he hadn't.
Now the hook was bare.
He crossed to the front door. It was not locked. It was not even shut. The latch rested against the strike plate without catching, and the door stood a finger's width open onto the night.
Rei had lived in this flat his whole life. He had never once known Gin to leave the door like that.

He pushed it open. The walkway outside was empty. The orange street lamp lit the railing, the bicycle stands and the row of closed doors, exactly as it did every night. Two doors down, a neighbour's futon was still hung over the rail to air. Nothing moved. The city went on being large and ordinary and indifferent, and somehow that was worse than if something had moved.
Something glinted on the concrete just past the threshold.

A key. A single brass door key on a plain ring, lying where a hand had dropped it or set it down. Rei crouched and picked it up. It was cold, properly cold, the cold of metal that has lain out all night. Beside it, crushed flat, lay the stub of a cigarette smoked exactly halfway.
Gin's brand. Gin smoked half a cigarette on the step every morning and stubbed it out, because Rei complained about the smell inside. He never smoked at night.

Rei looked left along the walkway, then right, down to the street. Empty. Asleep. Perfect. There was nothing else at all, and that was the part that would not leave him afterward. How completely nothing else there was.
He went back inside and shut the door, and this time he heard the latch catch.
It was only then that he saw the book on the kitchen table. He must have walked past it twice.

Gin's archive. The thick, soft-cornered field book Gin carried everywhere, into places Rei was not allowed to know about and out again, year after year. Gin did not leave it on tables. He did not leave it anywhere. And yet here it lay, open, squared to the edge of the table as if someone had wanted it found by the first person to sit down.
It was open at the first page. The handwriting was Gin's, small and exact, the print of a man who trusted ink more than memory. Rei read it standing up.

doc.title: Personal Archive. Opening Note
lines: If you found this: the keys were on the hook because I put them there. The lamp was on because I was working. The door was not quite closed because I heard something in the corridor and I looked up and then I kept writing and I forgot to go back and close it.

Whatever you are looking for... the world is in here. I documented everything I know. Six years of field work, case files, entity taxonomy, practitioner profiles, the political landscape of who controls what and why. The archive is complete. It functions without me.
Start at chapter one. Read in order the first time. The world builds on itself and some things will not make sense until other things do. The index is in the field kit, left pocket.
I was going to annotate the later sections more thoroughly. I ran out of time. The notes in the margins are the annotations. Read the margins.

blocks.p: Rei read it again. Then he looked up.
The lamp in Gin's room was burning. That part was true.
The front door had not been quite closed. That part was true.
The hook by the door was empty.

The note had been written for a night when Gin heard something in the corridor, looked up, and went back to his writing. It had not been written for a night when he got up from the table and went out to see what it was.

Rei turned the page with a hand that was not entirely steady. The next page was headed The World. It was dense, careful prose about apertures and membranes, the kind of thing Gin said at dinner when he was tired and forgot who he was talking to. Halfway down, a sentence stopped Rei so hard that he put his palm flat on the table.

doc.title: Personal Archive. The World
lines: The archive you are reading is set in the Kita district of the city. A specific apartment. A desk lamp that was on because I was working. A field investigator's archive, open on the desk.
If you are reading this at 3:47 in the morning: that is approximately when Rei found it. That detail is in the archive for a reason. Keep reading.

blocks.p: He looked at the stove clock. It said 3:52.

He made himself think it through slowly. Either Gin had known, weeks or months ago, at what hour of what night his brother would come to this table. Or somebody had written that line since. Rei did not know which was worse, and he found he did not want to know yet.

He closed the book. He put it in his bag. He put the cold key in his pocket, where it went on being cold against his leg. Then he let himself think the sentence all the way to the end, the one he had been holding off since the empty hook.
Something has happened to Gin.
There. It was in the room now. He could not put it back.

He could wait until morning and call the Division and let the proper people fail to find his brother. Nobody would blame him. Rei stood in the kitchen with the book heavy on his shoulder and knew he was not going to wait. He pulled on his shoes without untying them, the way Gin always told him not to.
Itsuki answered his message before he reached the bottom of the stairs.

Kuroda Itsuki was awake. Itsuki was always awake at this hour, painting or coding or both, and he had been Rei's best friend since they were twelve. Rei had typed four lines with his thumb while he locked the door. Gin didn't come home. Door was open. His key was on the walkway. I'm going down to Ōji.
I'm up, Itsuki wrote back. I was going to message you. He didn't answer me either, since Wednesday. Tell me what you need and I'll find it.

Rei did not need to say where he was going. They both knew Gin's way home. It ran down the long slope to the overpass at Ōji, and the overpass was the last place where anyone could say for certain that Gin had been ordinary.
Rei had crossed the Ōji overpass a thousand times without a thought. Tonight, halfway across, he walked into cold.

It was not a draught. It was a column of air that did not belong to August, standing in the middle of the walkway like a person waiting for someone. The hair rose on his arms. Under the noise of the first delivery trucks he heard something very small. A sound like a child trying not to cough.
He stopped.

Something was caught there. He could not have said how he knew. It was the same way he knew a room had just had an argument in it, or that a man on the train was about to cry. Gin used to call it noticing. Rei called it nothing at all, because it was just how his head worked.
The thing in the cold felt him notice it. It went very still, the way small animals go still when something large finally looks their way.
“It's all right,” Rei said under his breath, to nobody, to it. “I'm not going to do anything.”
He stood there with his hands in his pockets until the trucks had gone past. Slowly the cold thinned. Before it went, it let something go, the way a fist opens at the end.

It was not words. It was a picture, laid in his mind as clearly as a photograph. This bridge, at night. A man crossing it, walking north. The lamp behind him. And his shadow falling the wrong way. It did not stretch back toward the light. It lay ahead of him on the concrete, leading him, as though something walked half a second in front of the man it belonged to.
The night Gin stopped answering.
Then the cold was gone, and the overpass was only an overpass, and Rei was standing in the middle of it with his heart going hard.
He typed it into the notes on his phone before he could start doubting it. A man with the wrong shadow. Ōji overpass. The night Gin vanished.
Then he looked down.
The street lamp was behind him. His own shadow lay behind him too, long and thin, where a shadow belongs. He watched it for a long moment anyway, to be sure it stayed there.
His phone buzzed. Itsuki. Come to the studio. Don't walk back over the bridge.
A second message, a moment later. I think I've been painting it.
